topic.subject: science
topic.title: Health and disease
topic.scope: health vs disease, acute and chronic, infectious agents, modes of spread, prevention, immunisation

misconceptions.statement: If I do not have a specific disease like a cold or fever, I am a healthy person.
misconceptions.why: Students equate health only with the absence of physical symptoms.
misconceptions.fix: Health is a state of complete physical, mental, and social well-being, not just the absence of disease.

probe.question: If a person is physically fit but constantly stressed and unable to interact with others, are they healthy?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because they don't have any disease.

misconceptions.root_belief: absence of bad means presence of good

misconceptions.statement: Antibiotics are effective for curing the common cold and flu.
misconceptions.why: Students believe all 'germ-killing' medicines work on all types of germs.
misconceptions.fix: Antibiotics block biochemical pathways specific to bacteria; they do not work on viruses like those causing the cold.

probe.question: Why doesn't a doctor prescribe penicillin for a viral flu?
probe.wrong_answer: Because the flu is not a strong enough infection for antibiotics.

misconceptions.root_belief: one medicine fixes all similar symptoms

misconceptions.statement: Mosquitoes are the cause of malaria.
misconceptions.why: Students observe the mosquito bite leading to illness and ignore the microscopic pathogen.
misconceptions.fix: Mosquitoes are vectors that carry the malaria-causing protozoan (Plasmodium) from one person to another.

probe.question: If a mosquito that does not carry Plasmodium bites you, will you get malaria?

misconceptions.root_belief: the visible carrier is the primary cause

misconceptions.statement: Vaccines are a type of medicine given to cure a person who is already sick.
misconceptions.why: Students confuse the act of injection with the administration of curative drugs.
misconceptions.fix: Vaccines are preventive; they train the immune system to recognize a pathogen before an actual infection occurs.

probe.question: When should a person ideally receive a polio vaccine?
probe.wrong_answer: After they start showing symptoms of polio.

misconceptions.root_belief: prevention and cure are the same process

misconceptions.statement: All bacteria are harmful and cause diseases in humans.
misconceptions.why: The curriculum focuses on pathogenic bacteria, leading to a negative bias.
misconceptions.fix: Many bacteria are beneficial, such as those in our gut or those used to make curd.

probe.question: Are the bacteria found in human intestines considered a disease?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, all bacteria inside the body cause illness.

misconceptions.root_belief: a category is defined by its worst members

misconceptions.statement: You can only catch an infectious disease if you physically touch an infected person.
misconceptions.why: Students rely on visible evidence of contact to explain transmission.
misconceptions.fix: Infectious diseases can spread through air (droplets), water, food, or intermediate carriers like flies.

probe.question: How can you get a cold from someone sitting across the room without touching them?
probe.wrong_answer: You can't; you must have touched their hand or belongings.

misconceptions.root_belief: what you cannot see does not exist

misconceptions.statement: All diseases are caused by germs or external microorganisms.
misconceptions.why: Heavy emphasis on hygiene and 'germ theory' in early schooling.
misconceptions.fix: Many diseases are non-infectious, caused by genetic abnormalities, organ malfunction, or lifestyle factors.

probe.question: Is high blood pressure caused by a virus or bacteria?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, it must be a germ that entered the body.

misconceptions.root_belief: one effect has one single cause

misconceptions.statement: Reducing a fever with medicine means the disease is cured.
misconceptions.why: Students confuse the disappearance of a symptom with the elimination of the pathogen.
misconceptions.fix: Reducing symptoms like fever makes the patient comfortable, but the pathogen must still be killed to cure the disease.

probe.question: If you take paracetamol and your fever goes away, is the infection definitely gone?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because the fever was the disease.

misconceptions.root_belief: treating symptoms is the same as curing causes

misconceptions.statement: Chronic diseases are just acute diseases that haven't been treated yet.
misconceptions.why: Students think the only difference between diseases is how long they are ignored.
misconceptions.fix: Chronic diseases are fundamentally different in their progression and long-term impact on health compared to acute ones.

probe.question: If you don't treat a common cold, will it eventually turn into elephantiasis?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, any short disease becomes chronic if left alone.

misconceptions.root_belief: all diseases follow the same progression

misconceptions.statement: Vaccines are dangerous because they contain the actual disease-causing germ.
misconceptions.why: Literal interpretation of 'weakened' or 'dead' pathogens without understanding the immune response.
misconceptions.fix: Vaccines use killed or weakened microbes that mimic the pathogen to build immunity without causing the full disease.

probe.question: Why do we give a small dose of a weakened germ to a healthy child?
probe.wrong_answer: To make them slightly sick so they get used to it.

misconceptions.root_belief: a part behaves exactly like the whole

misconceptions.statement: Viruses are just a very small type of bacteria.
misconceptions.why: Both are microscopic and cause disease, leading students to group them together.
misconceptions.fix: Viruses and bacteria have completely different structures and life processes; viruses are not even considered fully 'living' by some.

probe.question: Can we use the same mechanism to kill both a virus and a bacteria?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because they are both tiny germs.

misconceptions.statement: Health is purely a personal matter and has nothing to do with the community.
misconceptions.why: Focus on individual biology rather than environmental and social factors.
misconceptions.fix: Individual health depends on community health, such as clean environment, garbage disposal, and social harmony.

probe.question: Can a person stay healthy if their neighborhood has open drains and uncollected trash?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, as long as they eat well and exercise personally.

misconceptions.root_belief: the individual is independent of the environment
